representations.text/plain: Options:InhibinEstrogenProgesteroneTestosteroneCorrect Answer: A) InhibinExplanation:Inhibin is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by Sertoli cells in males and Granulosa cells in females.Its primary function is to selectively inhibit FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.Estrogen (Option B)Estrogen can have both negative and positive feedback effects, depending on its concentration and timing.Low to moderate levels: inhibit both FSH and LH secretion via negative feedback.Jkdejkdjekdjekd deojdkejdkedJkdekdejdke dkejdkejdkedjkdejdkekdedSustained high levels (as in late follicular phase): cause positive feedback leading to LH surge.However, estrogen’s inhibition is not specific to FSH — it affects both gonadotropins.djkejdkejdkejdkeddkejdkedjkeddjkejdkedeDjkewjkdejdkeddejkdjkewjdkdjkedjdkejdkejdkejkejkdejdkedkdjekdjekdjkedekdekjdkjdedTestosterone (Option D)In males, testosterone exerts negative feedback mainly on the hypothalamus and pituitary to suppress LH secretion. It has little direct effect on FSH. Instead, inhibin from Sertoli cells is responsible for FSH suppression.Key Takeaways:Inhibin, secreted by Sertoli cells in males and Granulosa cells in females, specifically inhibits FSH secretion, not LH. Estrogen and progesterone affect both FSH and LH through negative feedback, though estrogen can also induce positive feedback at high levels. Testosterone primarily suppresses LH secretion, with little effect on FSH.Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, Page 897104.
